title: Europe entered winter with a thin gas buffer, while US refiners faced stronger competition for products
summary: The Dallas Fed's November Energy Indicators identifies two shortages with different implications for prices. In Europe and Asia, buyers were competing for LNG cargoes after conflict disrupted supplies from the Middle East and Russia. In the US, the pressure was particularly acute in finished diesel: higher refinery runs and softer domestic demand on some year-over-year comparisons had not rebuilt inventories because overseas demand absorbed additional barrels. Neither market can be understood from the price of US crude alone.

Europe was approaching the winter withdrawal season with 13% less gas in storage than a year earlier. The report puts the shortfall against the mean since the loss of most Russian supplies in 2022 at 28%. Chart 2 plots working gas in terawatt-hours and puts the 2026 trajectory alongside 2025 and two historical averages, for 2019–21 and 2023–25. Its red line ends as withdrawals begin. It gives no forecast of end-winter stocks. Recent mild winters, weaker industrial gas use and substitution towards coal had moderated prices since 2022. Those mechanisms could again temper withdrawals, even though the starting buffer was smaller.

The pressure was visible across importing regions. Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and damage to facilities constrained LNG exports, particularly from Qatar. European buyers bid for cargoes as shipping and insurance became more expensive. The report records a 64% July–October increase in Dutch TTF and a 53% increase in the Japan–Korea marker. Chart 1's labelled averages for the week of 30 October were $32.45 and $32.84 per MMBtu respectively, against $3.02 at Henry Hub. Within the US, Waha weakened as oil production in the Permian delivered more associated gas. The October dashboard separately gives a $2.99 Henry Hub average and a 3.47% July–October increase, while the accompanying discussion reports a 13% increase. The different displayed changes are not reconciled in the text. The international divergence is clear in the levels without choosing one US growth rate.

US export capacity provided a link between the markets. LNG shipments reached 17.7 billion cubic feet per day in September, up 17.4% from a year earlier. Pipeline exports also rose. The text reports 10.5 billion cubic feet per day, while the chart 3 label gives 10.2 for shipments to Canada and Mexico. The report does not explain the discrepancy. The shaded part of the chart shows EIA projections. By December 2027, the EIA expected LNG exports to rise by a further 4.6 billion cubic feet per day and pipeline exports by 0.4 from September levels, taking total exports from about 25% of US dry gas production to 27.4%. Market prices conveyed a different kind of information. In the week ending 13 November, the December 2027 Henry Hub contract averaged $3.95 per MMBtu against about $3.21 for December 2026. That $0.74 difference was observable in the futures curve. It neither guarantees the EIA volume forecast nor measures the separate effects of export demand, storage and risk premia.

In petroleum, the dashboard gives an October WTI average of $96.64 per barrel. Chart 4 compares crude and retail fuels in October 2026 dollars per gallon. From July to October, gasoline rose 8.4% to $4.45 a gallon and diesel rose 24.7% to $6.25. The article's inflation-adjusted per-gallon WTI series rose 25.5% to $2.43, a different measure from the dashboard's 22.37% increase. The report puts crude's recent share of retail diesel cost at 37%, down from roughly half. The remaining share includes costs between crude purchase and retail sale. It cannot all be attributed to refinery profit.

From June to September, gasoline, jet fuel and diesel use rose 2.4%, 2.2% and 3.2%, respectively, broadly following seasonal patterns. Diesel and jet fuel use were flat against a year earlier. October gross refinery inputs, meanwhile, rose 5.6% year over year. Third-quarter Gulf Coast crude processing exceeded the corresponding 2019 level by 2.4% even though refining capacity had been about 1.5 million barrels per day greater in 2019. More intensive use of the available system therefore coexisted with low inventories, especially of diesel (charts 4–5).

Chart 6 shows why the direction of crude exports is a poor guide to gasoline or diesel availability. Its crude series uses the right-hand scale and the three product series use the left. Crude exports fell 30% from May to August as Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases wound down. Over the same months gasoline exports rose 1.5%, while jet fuel and diesel exports fell 3.4% and 0.3%. The year-over-year comparison gives a different picture: August exports of the three finished fuels together were up about 0.6 million barrels per day, exceeding the 0.4 million decline in domestic use. The authors expect continued pressure on product prices relative to crude for as long as geopolitical conflicts keep substantial global refining capacity offline. A recovery in that capacity or weaker overseas demand would weaken the mechanism. The article supplies no spread target or trade recommendation.

questions.question: How far could EU storage fall under different winter demand paths?
questions.detail: The unusually low starting stock matters most if withdrawals accelerate while replacement cargoes remain scarce. Combine the working-gas data cited in chart 2 with weather-conditioned weekly consumption, industrial demand and confirmed LNG arrivals. The trajectory in physical units would help distinguish a price premium needed to attract marginal cargoes from one that could unwind in a mild winter.

questions.question: Can US exporters supply the additional LNG volumes on the projected schedule?
questions.detail: The EIA projection attributes much of future export growth to LNG. The observed calendar spread does not identify how much of that capacity the market expects to operate. Compare the cited Short-Term Energy Outlook with commissioning dates, realised feedgas demand, utilisation and deliverable pipeline capacity. Delays or a domestic supply response could change the exposure of Henry Hub to overseas shortages.

questions.question: How much of the diesel premium depends on export pull rather than a domestic bottleneck?
questions.detail: Refinery inputs were strong, but finished-fuel inventories remained low. National crude runs alone cannot locate a shortage in a particular product or region. Compare contemporaneous EIA distillate stocks, refinery yields, regional outages and export loadings over matched weeks. Recovery of foreign refining capacity alongside a narrowing product spread would support the authors' explanation more directly than a decline in outright crude prices.

limitation: The Dallas Fed flags possible revisions to earlier observations. The two differences between the dashboard, text and chart labels are described above.
